name: Chromewear Wednesday — The Aug Solidarity Dress Code
creator: Started by Shelf aug-worker collective 'The Bolted Saints,' Meridian East
description: Every Wednesday, participants wore their augmentations fully exposed — no skin coverage, no aesthetic casing, no polish — raw chrome, visible ports, unsheathed actuators, bare junction scars. The challenge was explicitly political: augmented workers who covered their chrome to appear 'more human' in corporate environments were encouraged to stop, treating Wednesday as a single day of refusal. Tier 1 and 2 participants began the trend; by its third month, it had spread to Tier 3 office workers and generated visible discomfort in Tier 4 corporate spaces.
medium: physical, neural feed documentation, live presence
cultural_impact: Chromewear Wednesday reframed augmentation visibility as a labor rights issue rather than an aesthetic choice, contributing directly to the language of subsequent Chrome Mandate opposition movements and normalizing raw-chrome aesthetics across tier boundaries in ways that persist to the present.
controversy: Several Tier 3-4 employers issued internal dress codes explicitly prohibiting 'unhoused augmentation' on grounds of 'workplace professionalism,' which were leaked to pirate feeds and became recruitment tools for labor organizing. One Tier 4 compliance officer's memo went viral under the title 'The Machine Doesn't Dress for You.'
story_hooks: The original Bolted Saints collective has fractured; one faction is selling the Wednesday brand to a Tier 4 fashion house and the other will do anything to stop them.
A character who participated in early Chromewear Wednesdays is now a Tier 4 middle manager who quietly enforces the dress codes they once refused — someone is about to remind them publicly.
A Tier 5 fashion designer has appropriated the raw-chrome aesthetic for a luxury line; the Bolted Saints want the profit and the apology.
